stem: When planning emergency egress and evacuation for a multi-story building, which practice best supports safety for people with disabilities?

options.text: Directing occupants to use the standard stairs, with large-print evacuation maps and floor wardens on each landing.
options.shortLabel: Standard stairs, large-print maps, and floor wardens
options.rationale: Standard stairs remain unusable for many people with disabilities, and maps plus floor wardens do not replace refuge areas, evacuation devices, or visual alarms.

options.text: Providing areas of refuge with two-way communication, evacuation chairs, and alarms that use both sound and light.
options.shortLabel: Refuge areas, evacuation chairs, and multisensory alarms
options.rationale: Safe egress requires multisensory alarms (audible and visible), two-way communication in areas of refuge, and a way to assist people who cannot use stairs.

options.text: Installing audible and visual alarms, posting tactile maps, and telling occupants who cannot use stairs to take the elevator down.
options.shortLabel: Alarms, tactile maps, and elevator evacuation
options.rationale: Visual alarms and tactile maps help with notification, but standard elevators are not a safe evacuation route in a fire.

options.text: Posting tactile evacuation maps at each area of refuge, in the main lobby, and on the staff intranet portal.
options.shortLabel: Tactile maps at refuge, lobby, and intranet
options.rationale: Maps alone do not provide notification or assisted evacuation, and an intranet portal is not available to occupants during an emergency.

explanation: An accessible evacuation plan addresses notification, egress, and assisted rescue. Emergency warning systems should provide both audible and visible alerts, and areas of refuge should have accessible two-way communication so occupants can call for help. Emergency stair travel devices, such as evacuation chairs, can assist people who cannot use stairs.

references.title: Emergency Evacuation Planning Guide for People with Disabilities
references.author: NFPA
